parts.move: state the qualitative law for the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field
parts.prompt: State the three factors that set the size of the force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field, and describe the force's direction.
scheme: Field strength (flux density B)
Current I, and the length of wire in the field
The angle to the field (sinθ dependence)
Perpendicular to both the wire and the field (Fleming's left-hand rule)
parts.answer: The force grows with flux density, current and in-field wire length, and scales as sinθ with the angle between current and field. Its direction is at right angles to both — Fleming's left-hand rule maps thumb, first and second finger to force, field and current.

parts.move: state how the force on a moving charge differs from that on a current-carrying wire
parts.prompt: State the factors determining the magnetic force on a moving charge, and the two ways it differs in direction from the force on a current-carrying wire.
scheme: F = BQv sinθ: charge, speed, flux density, angle
The force is perpendicular to both the velocity and the field
Opposite charges feel opposite forces; conventional current already folds in the sign
parts.answer: A moving charge feels F = BQv sinθ — same geometry as the wire, but two differences bite: the force depends on the charge's sign (an electron deflects opposite to a proton), and it is perpendicular to the velocity, which is why it steers without ever speeding up the particle.

parts.move: explain the wire force as the sum of forces on its drifting charges
parts.prompt: The force on a current-carrying wire is sometimes called 'the charge force on a bigger scale'. Explain this, sketching how the microscopic picture produces F = BIl.
scheme: A current is many drifting charges, each feeling BQv
The charges pass their sideways push to the lattice through collisions
Summed over all carriers: NqAv_d × Bv_d → BIl
The wire force is literally the collective of the individual charge forces
parts.answer: Each drifting electron feels BQv sideways. The electrons cannot leave the metal, so they hand that push to the lattice in countless collisions. Summed over all carriers, NqAv_d × Bv_d → BIl: the wire force is literally the collective of the individual charge forces. The motor's torque is not a new force; it is the charge force with a payroll.

parts.move: explain why the magnetic force must be perpendicular to both field and motion
parts.prompt: Explain why the magnetic force lies perpendicular to the field AND perpendicular to the current/velocity, and what would violate that if it pointed any other way.
scheme: A component along the wire/current would do work on the carriers — impossible for a force arising from a static field
A component along B would make 'parallel' and 'antiparallel' motions feel different sideways pushes — no experimental basis
The unique geometry satisfying the observations (no work, symmetric dependence) is perpendicular to both — the cross-product structure
parts.answer: Any force along the current would do work on charges, which a steady magnetic field never does; any force along the field would treat the two field directions inequivalently, which experiments deny. The only geometry that fits every observation is perpendicularity to both — F = BQv sinθ, direction by the right-hand rule — and nature insists on it: the force is exactly a cross product.

parts.move: invert BIl to size a voice coil: work out the wire length the geometry offers and the turns needed for a target force
parts.prompt: A loudspeaker must exert 0.50 N on its coil in a 0.15 T radial field with 1.0 A through the wire. Each turn of the 2.5 cm-diameter former contributes one circumference of wire. How many turns does the coil need?
scheme: Required BIl product: l = F/(BI) = 0.50/(0.15×1.0) = 3.33 m of wire in the field
One turn supplies πd = π×0.025 = 0.0785 m
≈ 43 turns (round up: 42 turns fall just short)
parts.answer: The force target demands l = F/(BI) = 0.50/(0.15×1) = 3.3 m of current-carrying wire. A 2.5 cm former gives 7.85 cm per turn, so 3.33/0.0785 ≈ 43 turns. The designer works backwards from the force through the geometry.

parts.move: apply F = BQv to find the force on a beam electron
parts.prompt: An electron travels at 3.0×10⁷ m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a 4.0 mT field. Calculate the force on it, and compare it with the electron's weight. (e = 1.60×10⁻¹⁹ C, m_e = 9.11×10⁻³¹ kg, g = 9.81 m s⁻²)
scheme: Magnetic force exceeds weight by ~10¹⁵ — gravity is laughably irrelevant here
parts.answer: The field deflects the electron with BQv = 1.9×10⁻¹⁴ N. Its entire weight is 8.9×10⁻³⁰ N — the magnetic push is fifteen orders of magnitude stronger. This is the arithmetic reason CRT and electron-optics textbooks never mention gravity.

parts.move: correct confusion between the motor rule and the generator rule
parts.prompt: A student uses Fleming's left-hand rule to find the current produced by a spinning generator coil. Explain the mix-up and name the right rule for each machine.
scheme: Left-hand rule: motion of a current (motor effect) — given current and field, find force
Right-hand rule: current from motion (generator) — given force/motion and field, find induced current
The two are different problems: one finds effect of current, the other finds effect of motion
parts.answer: Left hand answers 'which way does a current-carrying wire get pushed?' — the motor question. The generator asks the reverse, 'which current does this motion produce?' — the right-hand (or Lenz-law) question. Both machines share the same field and current, but the roles of cause and effect are swapped, and the student's left hand reads the right-hand problem.

parts.move: reject the idea that a parallel field-current arrangement still gives a force
parts.prompt: A wire carries current straight along a 2.0 T field line, and a student predicts F = BIl = 1.0 N for a 0.50 m, 1.0 A wire. Calculate the true force and explain the error.
scheme: The full law is F = BIl sinθ
θ = 0 (current along field) → sinθ = 0
True force = 0 N, not 1.0 N
parts.answer: The formula the student skipped is F = BIl sinθ: with the current running along the field, sin 0° = 0 and the force vanishes. The field only pushes charges that cut across it — sliding along field lines is magnetically invisible.

parts.move: balance magnetic force against weight to find a levitation current
parts.prompt: A horizontal wire of mass 0.012 kg and length 0.30 m lies perpendicular to a 0.60 T field. Calculate the current needed to levitate it. (g = 9.81 m s⁻²)
scheme: Set BIl = mg
parts.answer: Levitation needs BIl = mg, so I = 0.012×9.81/(0.60×0.30) ≈ 0.65 A in the right direction. A modest current, but the field must hold the wire perpendicular and the current exactly right — drift either and the balance tips.

parts.move: compute the helix radius from a charge's perpendicular velocity component
parts.prompt: A proton enters a 0.20 T field with speed 5.0×10⁶ m s⁻¹ at 30° to the field. Calculate the radius of its helical path and the pitch of the helix. (m_p = 1.67×10⁻²⁷ kg, e = 1.60×10⁻¹⁹ C)
parts.answer: Only the perpendicular component circles: r = mv sinθ/Bq = 0.13 m. The period T = 2πm/Bq = 0.33 μs is set by the field alone, so the parallel 4.3×10⁶ m s⁻¹ carries the proton 1.4 m along the field each turn. The helix is a circle and a straight line superposed — the field cannot touch the parallel part.

parts.move: use the radius-mass relation r = mv/Bq as a sorting principle to separate isotopes
parts.prompt: Singly ionised ²⁰Ne and ²²Ne atoms, both travelling at 1.0×10⁵ m s⁻¹, enter a 0.10 T field perpendicularly. Calculate each orbit radius and explain how this sorts isotopes. (m₂₀ ≈ 3.32×10⁻²⁶ kg, m₂₂ ≈ 3.65×10⁻²⁶ kg, e = 1.60×10⁻¹⁹ C)
scheme: r = mv/(Bq)
The heavier isotope turns wider — their landing points differ by 2(r₂₂ − r₂₀) = 4 cm; a detector plate sorts them
parts.answer: At the same speed and charge, r = mv/Bq grows with mass: 0.21 m for ²⁰Ne, 0.23 m for ²²Ne. After their semicircles the beams land 4 cm apart — enough to collect them separately. Magnetic sorting by inertia is exactly how mass spectrometers separate isotopes.

parts.move: explain the Hall effect's transverse voltage as the steady state of magnetic and electric forces balancing
parts.prompt: A current flows along a thin metal strip placed in a field perpendicular to it, and a voltage develops across the strip's width. Explain, in terms of forces on charges, why the Hall voltage appears and what it measures.
scheme: The field pushes the drifting charges sideways (BQv)
They accumulate on one edge until the built-up charge's electric force balances the magnetic push
That equilibrium gives eE_H = BQv_d, so the Hall voltage measures B
Swap the current or field direction and the voltage sign reverses
parts.answer: The field shoves the drifting charges sideways (BQv), and they accumulate on one edge until the built-up charge's electric force balances the magnetic push. At equilibrium eE_H = BQv_d, so the Hall voltage measures B. Swap the current or field direction and the voltage sign reverses; it is a direct field meter.

parts.move: combine motor-effect forces with moments to explain a moving-coil meter
parts.prompt: A moving-coil meter has 100 turns of 2.0 cm × 1.5 cm coil in a 0.20 T radial field, on a spring of constant 2.4×10⁻⁴ N m rad⁻¹. Calculate the current that deflects the pointer 60°.
scheme: Force per pair of sides: each active side BIl, torque from the pair = BIl×width per turn
Total torque = NBIl × 0.015 m (radial field: torque angle-independent)
Spring torque = kθ = 2.4×10⁻⁴ × π/3 = 2.51×10⁻⁴ N m
parts.answer: Each of the 100 turns feels BIl on two sides, and the radial field keeps that torque steady at every angle. Balancing magnetic torque NBIl×0.015 against the spring's kθ at 60° gives I ≈ 4.2×10⁻² A, or 42 mA. The whole meter is F = BIl wearing a moment's clothing, and the radial field is what makes its scale linear.

parts.move: combine the charge-force law with electric force balance to select a speed
parts.prompt: In a region where a 0.040 T field points into the page, a 2.0×10⁵ V m⁻¹ electric field points upward. A positive ion of charge e crosses perpendicular to both and is undeflected. Calculate its speed, and explain why ions of different mass and different charge pass together provided they share that speed.
scheme: Electric force qE upward; magnetic force qvB downward when v points right
Undeflected: qE = qvB → v = E/B = 2.0×10⁵/0.040 = 5.0×10⁶ m s⁻¹
q cancels — the selector is mass- and charge-blind
Only speed matters: any charge-to-mass ratio passes if it crosses at E/B
parts.answer: Balancing qE against qvB gives v = E/B = 5.0×10⁶ m s⁻¹. The charge cancels on both sides, so every undeflected particle crosses at exactly this speed — heavy ions, light ions, singly or doubly charged, all pass together. After this gate, any further deflection by a field is pure mass-to-charge bookkeeping: the selector is the entrance, not the spectrometer.
